title: Because It's Not Fun Enough
excerpt: Andrew Oram asked why programming languages rise and fall, and quoted the answer without noticing. Programming is a vocation, an art, and a job. Make any of those harder than they need to be, and your language survives exactly as long as it can't be replaced.
content_html:
Andrew Oram wrote a two-part series for the Linux Professional Institute asking why programming languages rise and fall (parts one and two.) It says, roughly, that C, C++, and JavaScript are immortal (for now!), with Java a maybe; COBOL, FORTRAN, BASIC, and Perl lived respectable lives and got sent upstate to retire on a farm; Pascal, Objective-C, PL/I, Ada, and Tcl were false starts, with Ruby somewhere on the bubble. It's a good tour from a man who has been editing this industry's books forever, and near the end of it, Oram quotes Simon Peyton Jones, who observes that a language's adoption is "very weakly connected to its technical merits," and that the social and economic factors do the actual deciding.

That quote is the article, and it's a little surprising that it's buried so far into the content; maybe engineering for human nature makes it difficult to make that quote the leading thesis because we don't want to read that quite so bluntly, but it's true.

Language adoption is not solely technical - it's technical and human.

Everything in the two parts before that quote is evidence for the sentiment, assembled but never organized as evidence. The series sorts languages by outcome: immortal, respectable, and failed. The interesting sort is by cause of death, and the causes come out of a simple observation that Peyton Jones compresses and Oram circles: programming is done by people, and for people it is three things at once. It is a vocation, an art, and a job. A language serves someone practicing all three, and a language or tool that makes any of the three unnecessarily difficult will not survive past the moment it can be replaced.

A vocation is a calling the world happens to pay for: something someone would do anyway, paycheck or no paycheck. An art is something someone does out of love and (hopefully) skill, and a job is the daily work, the thing someone does so they can eat and watch TV and sleep under a roof and boring stuff like that.

Musicians live this triple identity every working day: the covers set is the job, the originals are the art, and the vocation is what puts an instrument in their hands every day, booked or not. Programmers live it too; we just don't say it out loud as often.

Sort the corpses that way and they separate cleanly.

Some languages failed as a job: standard Pascal shipped without a usable string type and Tcl couldn't carry programs past a certain weight, so the daily work was harder than it had to be.1

Some failed as an art: Ada and PL/I were chosen for programmers rather than by them, languages of mandate, and nobody has ever loved a mandate.

Some failed as a vocation: Perl's job market walked to Python and didn't come back2, and Haskell famously set out to avoid success at all costs, a goal it achieved3.

Different diseases, one pathology. In every case somebody made one of the three axes needlessly difficult, and the people the language depended on went where it was easier, or more fun, or more workable.

A language that makes life hard will not survive past the moment it can be replaced. That statement explains every anomaly on Oram's list. JavaScript fails as an art for a large share of the people writing it, and it survives anyway, because it remains the browser's main general-purpose language4. Objective-C was awkward as both art and job, and it thrived for fifteen years because it was the only door into the most lucrative developer ecosystem ever built; the moment Swift existed, it evaporated and now survives as a shadow, preserved in its descendant. COBOL survives because replacing it is too difficult and expensive - something some companies are noticing and trying to address. If they succeed, COBOL is likely gone: a language that works 100% of the time and is about 1% fun to program. Ada survives today where certification regimes made it nearly irreplaceable5. Its difficulty is a standing eviction notice. It gets served on the day an alternative shows up, and not one day sooner.

Which leaves C++ looming, difficult and immortal, apparently contradicting all of this. Rust too, difficult by design and rising. The thing is that there are two kinds of difficulty, and the series conflates them.

One kind of difficulty is the violin's: precise, demanding, and chosen because it is precise and demanding. People do codegolf in C++ for sport. People write essays about the day the borrow checker finally clicked, the way string players talk about the day vibrato stopped being a fight. Difficulty itself isn't fatal; difficulty without sufficient return is. C++ and Rust have that return, just as the violin does.

The other kind of difficulty is friction: Ada's compliance apparatus, standard Pascal's missing pieces6, COBOL's amazing and precise and demanding structural syntax that doesn't actually create program structure much at all. Nobody ever wrote an essay about the day Ada's paperwork clicked. That difficulty hits all three axes for... what? Nothing. Ada and C++ both read as "hard languages" in a survey. But Ada dies as a standard language and C++ survives today because the "hard" parts were on different axes.

And where is Java in all of this? Good question! Java isn't as difficult as C++ or Rust, so it doesn't need their defense: it's sort of immortal from utility AND fun right now, with a lot of passion restored to the ecosystem thanks to the recent improvements in packaging and features. But that's an entirely personal decision on the part of the programmer; I think it's safe to say Java ain't dying quite yet, but it's hard to say why or when: I'm personally living in Java-land day by day. I'm biased.

Back to music, then, where the analogy stops being an analogy. A modern sampler can reproduce every note a violin makes. It can reproduce every nuance a violin makes; it is an encyclopedia of techniques, bowings, articulations, the works. And getting it to actually do all of that is more work than just playing the violin itself7! The capability was never the question. It turns out that the best way to get a sound like a violin being played is actually playing the violin. This is also, quietly, why code exists: a program is a compact specification for behavior, and describing behavior in prose costs more than the notation built for the job8.

I can get a computer to play guitar for me, and I can make it play much as I do on guitar: I know how I play, I understand my own preferences and accents. I can replicate my playing on guitar, gesture by gesture, note by note. And it is no fun. None. The result is fine; the doing is gone, and the doing was the point. There is no life to it, even if I introduce randomization or use my own timings. This fails along the same three axes as everything else we've mentioned here.

For the person who only wants the notes, the sampler wins the job outright, completely. It will never play the wrong thing or at the wrong moment. For the person playing, it fails, because driving it costs more than playing, and it never touches the art at all. Which is why, when I want guitar on a track, I still reach for the guitar. Choosing it is the point. The law that sorts programming languages sorts their successors too. No special pleading required... or allowed.

So: why do programming languages rise and fall? Peyton Jones already said it, and Oram already quoted it. Languages don't lose benchmark fights. They lose people. They rise when they make the vocation, the art, and the job lighter, and they fall on the day something else can carry the same weight, because at that moment the only question left is... is it fun?9

  1. An aside on Pascal, because the false start is... slightly misleading. Pascal's commercial life didn't end in the classroom; it moved to Borland, where Turbo Pascal and then Delphi dominated PC development for over a decade. Turbo Pascal's author was Anders Hejlsberg, who went on to build Delphi, then C#, then TypeScript, while Wirth's own line ran through Oberon into Go by way of his student Robert Griesemer. Pascal didn't fall so much as get metabolized, which suits Oram's own observation that some languages win by influence rather than adoption. Also: I loved Pascal.

    ↩

  2. Somewhat helped by Larry Wall deciding that goalposts were meant to be moved: Perl spent two decades waiting for "Perl 6, any day now," so long that Perl 6 eventually became a different language entirely (Raku), while Parrot, the VM built to carry it, died waiting. Which... does anyone use Raku? I had to look up even what this one was named. I'm sure someone does, but... I bet if I asked a general forum if anyone used Perl, Python, or Raku, Perl and Python would get a lot of hands raised but Raku would get some questions, until people realized that it is Perl, sort of.

    ↩

  3. This is unfair, and I know it! It was "avoid success-at-all-costs," not "avoid success at all costs," an emphasis on priority, not failure. It meant that Haskell had design idioms it was not willing to sacrifice just to become more popular.

    ↩

  4. Ask Java about languages that run in the browser! ... just don't do it in the browser, because Java doesn't run there natively - you need a runtime like CheerpJ, which puts a JVM in the browser, or a compile-to-WebAssembly toolchain for that.

    ↩

  5. Ada's fascinating. It's quite powerful, it's mandated for some environments, and those mandates rest on good reasons: safety, precision, provability. But I've never once wanted to write it, and the Ada programmers I know describe it as a requirement of industry and fiat rather than a choice. Meanwhile Rust fulfills the mandate's reasons at least as well, and people are passionate about using it. Nobody had to write a procurement directive to make the borrow checker happen. Ada earned its niche by dictate; Rust is earning the same niche by preference, with only decades of momentum in the way, much as any COBOL replacement would face. This is conjecture, in that neither Ada nor COBOL is suffering mass replacement yet, but even so: this is the whole point.

    ↩

  6. I tried writing some Pascal not too long ago, and it was truly amusing how much I'd forgotten - and how much Pascal's difficulties were addressed by companies like Borland trying to make it usable.

    ↩

  7. This is utterly true. Most of electronic music has been built around trying to replicate in hardware techniques that come from actual human hands: aftertouch, X-Y controllers, breath controllers, tactile controllers, theremins... and this is not an exhaustive list at all. All to do something a dime-store guitar can do in the hands of a moderately-skilled guitarist.

    ↩

  8. This is, of course, why so many programs struggle: they express specifications that are, in the end, unclear.

    ↩

blocks.html_en: Different diseases, one pathology. In every case somebody made one of the three axes needlessly difficult, and the people the language depended on went where it was easier, or more fun, or more workable.

sentences.en: Different diseases, one pathology.
sentences.zh: 不同的疾病，一种病理。

sentences.en: In every case somebody made one of the three axes needlessly difficult, and the people the language depended on went where it was easier, or more fun, or more workable.
sentences.zh: 在每种情况下，都会有人使这三个轴中的一个变得不必要的困难，而该语言所依赖的人则去了更容易、或更有趣或更可行的地方。

blocks.html_en: A language that makes life hard will not survive past the moment it can be replaced. That statement explains every anomaly on Oram's list. JavaScript fails as an art for a large share of the people writing it, and it survives anyway, because it remains the browser's main general-purpose language4. Objective-C was awkward as both art and job, and it thrived for fifteen years because it was the only door into the most lucrative developer ecosystem ever built; the moment Swift existed, it evaporated and now survives as a shadow, preserved in its descendant. COBOL survives because replacing it is too difficult and expensive - something some companies are noticing and trying to address. If they succeed, COBOL is likely gone: a language that works 100% of the time and is about 1% fun to program. Ada survives today where certification regimes made it nearly irreplaceable5. Its difficulty is a standing eviction notice. It gets served on the day an alternative shows up, and not one day sooner.

sentences.en: A language that makes life hard will not survive past the moment it can be replaced.
sentences.zh: 一种让生活变得艰难的语言一旦被取代，就无法生存。

sentences.en: That statement explains every anomaly on Oram's list.
sentences.zh: 这句话解释了奥拉姆名单上的每一个异常现象。

sentences.en: JavaScript fails as an art for a large share of the people writing it, and it survives anyway, because it remains the browser's main general-purpose language4.
sentences.zh: 对于大部分编写它的人来说，JavaScript 作为一门艺术是失败的，但无论如何它仍然存在，因为它仍然是浏览器的主要通用语言4。

sentences.en: Objective-C was awkward as both art and job, and it thrived for fifteen years because it was the only door into the most lucrative developer ecosystem ever built; the moment Swift existed, it evaporated and now survives as a shadow, preserved in its descendant.
sentences.zh: Objective-C 无论是作为艺术还是作为工作都显得尴尬，但它繁荣了十五年，因为它是进入有史以来最赚钱的开发者生态系统的唯一大门；从 Swift 存在的那一刻起，它就消失了，现在以影子的形式存在，保留在它的后代中。

sentences.zh: COBOL 之所以能生存下来，是因为替换它太困难且昂贵——一些公司已经注意到这一点并试图解决这一问题。

sentences.zh: Ada 至今仍然存在，认证制度使其几乎不可替代5。

sentences.en: Its difficulty is a standing eviction notice.

sentences.en: It gets served on the day an alternative shows up, and not one day sooner.
sentences.zh: 它会在替代方案出现的当天提供，而不是早一天。

blocks.html_en: Which leaves C++ looming, difficult and immortal, apparently contradicting all of this. Rust too, difficult by design and rising. The thing is that there are two kinds of difficulty, and the series conflates them.

sentences.en: Which leaves C++ looming, difficult and immortal, apparently contradicting all of this.

sentences.en: Rust too, difficult by design and rising.
sentences.zh: Rust 也是如此，设计上很困难并且正在上升。

sentences.en: The thing is that there are two kinds of difficulty, and the series conflates them.

blocks.html_en: One kind of difficulty is the violin's: precise, demanding, and chosen because it is precise and demanding. People do codegolf in C++ for sport. People write essays about the day the borrow checker finally clicked, the way string players talk about the day vibrato stopped being a fight. Difficulty itself isn't fatal; difficulty without sufficient return is. C++ and Rust have that return, just as the violin does.

sentences.en: Difficulty itself isn't fatal; difficulty without sufficient return is.
sentences.zh: 困难本身并不致命；困难本身并不致命。没有足够回报的困难是。

sentences.en: C++ and Rust have that return, just as the violin does.
sentences.zh: C++ 和 Rust 都有这样的回报，就像小提琴一样。

blocks.html_en: The other kind of difficulty is friction: Ada's compliance apparatus, standard Pascal's missing pieces6, COBOL's amazing and precise and demanding structural syntax that doesn't actually create program structure much at all. Nobody ever wrote an essay about the day Ada's paperwork clicked. That difficulty hits all three axes for... what? Nothing. Ada and C++ both read as "hard languages" in a survey. But Ada dies as a standard language and C++ survives today because the "hard" parts were on different axes.

blocks.html_en: And where is Java in all of this? Good question! Java isn't as difficult as C++ or Rust, so it doesn't need their defense: it's sort of immortal from utility AND fun right now, with a lot of passion restored to the ecosystem thanks to the recent improvements in packaging and features. But that's an entirely personal decision on the part of the programmer; I think it's safe to say Java ain't dying quite yet, but it's hard to say why or when: I'm personally living in Java-land day by day. I'm biased.

blocks.html_en: Back to music, then, where the analogy stops being an analogy. A modern sampler can reproduce every note a violin makes. It can reproduce every nuance a violin makes; it is an encyclopedia of techniques, bowings, articulations, the works. And getting it to actually do all of that is more work than just playing the violin itself7! The capability was never the question. It turns out that the best way to get a sound like a violin being played is actually playing the violin. This is also, quietly, why code exists: a program is a compact specification for behavior, and describing behavior in prose costs more than the notation built for the job8.

sentences.zh: 那么，回到音乐，类比就不再是类比了。

blocks.html_en: I can get a computer to play guitar for me, and I can make it play much as I do on guitar: I know how I play, I understand my own preferences and accents. I can replicate my playing on guitar, gesture by gesture, note by note. And it is no fun. None. The result is fine; the doing is gone, and the doing was the point. There is no life to it, even if I introduce randomization or use my own timings. This fails along the same three axes as everything else we've mentioned here.

blocks.html_en: For the person who only wants the notes, the sampler wins the job outright, completely. It will never play the wrong thing or at the wrong moment. For the person playing, it fails, because driving it costs more than playing, and it never touches the art at all. Which is why, when I want guitar on a track, I still reach for the guitar. Choosing it is the point. The law that sorts programming languages sorts their successors too. No special pleading required... or allowed.

blocks.html_en: So: why do programming languages rise and fall? Peyton Jones already said it, and Oram already quoted it. Languages don't lose benchmark fights. They lose people. They rise when they make the vocation, the art, and the job lighter, and they fall on the day something else can carry the same weight, because at that moment the only question left is... is it fun?9

• An aside on Pascal, because the false start is... slightly misleading. Pascal's commercial life didn't end in the classroom; it moved to Borland, where Turbo Pascal and then Delphi dominated PC development for over a decade. Turbo Pascal's author was Anders Hejlsberg, who went on to build Delphi, then C#, then TypeScript, while Wirth's own line ran through Oberon into Go by way of his student Robert Griesemer. Pascal didn't fall so much as get metabolized, which suits Oram's own observation that some languages win by influence rather than adoption. Also: I loved Pascal.

content_html_zh:
Andrew Oram 为 Linux Professional Institute 撰写了一个由两部分组成的系列文章，询问编程语言为何兴衰（第一部分和第二部分）。 粗略地说，C、C++ 和 JavaScript 是不朽的（就目前而言！），而 Java 或许是不朽的。 COBOL、FORTRAN、BASIC 和 Perl 过着体面的生活，并被送到州北部的一个农场退休； Pascal、Objective-C、PL/I、Ada 和 Tcl 都是错误的开始，而 Ruby 则处于泡沫之中。 对于一个一直在编辑这个行业书籍的人来说，这是一次很好的游览，在接近尾声时，奥拉姆引用了西蒙·佩顿·琼斯 (Simon Peyton Jones) 的话，他指出，一种语言的采用“与其技术优点的联系非常微弱”，而社会和经济因素才是真正的决定因素。

这句话就是这篇文章，令人有点惊讶的是它被深深地埋藏在内容中；也许人性工程使得很难将这句话引用为主要论点，因为我们不想如此直白地阅读它，但这是事实。

语言的采用不仅仅是技术性的——它是技术性的和人性的。

该引文之前的两部分中的所有内容都是该观点的证据，它们被组合在一起，但从未被组织为证据。 该系列按照结果对语言进行分类：不朽的、受人尊敬的和失败的。 有趣的分类是按死亡原因分类，其原因来自 Peyton Jones 压缩和 Oram 圈子的一个简单观察：编程是由人完成的，对于人来说，它同时是三件事。 这是一种职业、一种艺术、一种工作。 一种语言服务于同时练习这三种语言的人，而一种使这三种语言中的任何一种都变得不必要的困难的语言或工具在被取代后就无法生存。

职业是一种召唤，世界碰巧为此付出了代价：某人无论如何都会做的事情，无论有没有薪水。 艺术是某人出于热爱和（希望）技能而做的事情，而工作是日常工作，是人们做的事情，这样他们就可以吃饭、看电视、在屋顶下睡觉以及诸如此类的无聊事情。

音乐家的每个工作日都经历着这种三重身份：封面设置是工作，原作是艺术，职业是每天将乐器放在他们手中，无论是否预订。 程序员也是如此。我们只是不经常大声说出来。

这样把尸体分类，它们就干净地分开了。

有些语言作为一项工作失败了：标准 Pascal 出厂时没有可用的字符串类型，而 Tcl 无法承载超过一定重量的程序，因此日常工作比应有的要困难。1

有些作为一门艺术失败了：Ada 和 PL/I 是为程序员选择的，而不是由他们选择的，它们是强制语言，而且从来没有人喜欢强制语言。

有些职业失败了：Perl 的就业市场转向了 Python，却再也没有回来2，而 Haskell 则不惜一切代价避免成功，但它实现了这一目标。

不同的疾病，一种病理。 在每种情况下，都会有人使这三个轴中的一个变得不必要的困难，而该语言所依赖的人则去了更容易、或更有趣或更可行的地方。

一种让生活变得艰难的语言一旦被取代，就无法生存。 这句话解释了奥拉姆名单上的每一个异常现象。 对于大部分编写它的人来说，JavaScript 作为一门艺术是失败的，但无论如何它仍然存在，因为它仍然是浏览器的主要通用语言4。 Objective-C 无论是作为艺术还是作为工作都显得尴尬，但它繁荣了十五年，因为它是进入有史以来最赚钱的开发者生态系统的唯一大门；从 Swift 存在的那一刻起，它就消失了，现在以影子的形式存在，保留在它的后代中。 COBOL 之所以能生存下来，是因为替换它太困难且昂贵——一些公司已经注意到这一点并试图解决这一问题。 如果他们成功了，COBOL 很可能就会消失：一种 100% 的时间都能工作、编程乐趣只有 1% 的语言。 Ada 至今仍然存在，认证制度使其几乎不可替代5。 它的困难在于长期驱逐通知。 它会在替代方案出现的当天提供，而不是早一天。

这使得 C++ 显得若隐若现、困难重重且不朽，显然与这一切相矛盾。 Rust 也是如此，设计上很困难并且正在上升。 问题是有两种难度，而该系列将它们混为一谈。

其中一种难度是小提琴的：精确、要求高，因为它精确且要求高而选择它。 人们用 C++ 进行代码高尔夫是为了运动。 人们写文章讲述借用检查器终于点击的那一天，弦乐演奏者谈论颤音不再是一场战斗的那一天。 困难本身并不致命；困难本身并不致命。没有足够回报的困难是。 C++ 和 Rust 都有这样的回报，就像小提琴一样。

另一种困难是摩擦：Ada 的合规性装置、标准 Pascal 的缺失部分6、COBOL 令人惊奇、精确且要求严格的结构语法，实际上根本无法创建太多程序结构。 从来没有人写过一篇关于艾达的文书工作成功的那一天的文章。 这个困难涉及所有三个轴...... 什么？ 没有什么。 在一项调查中，Ada 和 C++ 都被视为“硬语言”。 但 Ada 作为标准语言已经消亡，而 C++ 至今仍然存在，因为“困难”部分位于不同的轴上。

Java 在这一切中又处于什么位置呢？ 好问题！ Java 不像 C++ 或 Rust 那样困难，所以它不需要他们的防御：它现在从实用性和乐趣来看是不朽的，由于最近在包装和功能方面的改进，生态系统恢复了很多热情。 但这完全是程序员个人的决定；我认为可以肯定地说 Java 还没有消亡，但很难说为什么或何时消亡：我个人日复一日地生活在 Java 的土地上。 我有偏见。

那么，回到音乐，类比就不再是类比了。 现代采样器可以再现小提琴发出的每个音符。 它可以再现小提琴的每一个细微差别；它是一部技巧、弓法、演奏法和作品的百科全书。 让它真正完成所有这些工作比仅仅拉小提琴本身需要更多的工作7！ 能力从来都不是问题。 事实证明，获得小提琴演奏声音的最佳方法就是实际拉小提琴。 这也是代码存在的原因：程序是行为的紧凑规范，用散文描述行为的成本比为工作构建的符号要高8。

我可以让一台电脑为我弹吉他，我可以让它像我弹吉他一样弹奏：我知道我如何弹奏，我了解我自己的喜好和口音。 我可以复制我的吉他演奏，一个手势一个手势，一个音符一个音符。 这一点也不好玩。 没有任何。 结果很好；做的事情已经过去了，做的事情才是重点。 即使我引入随机化或使用我自己的计时，它也没有生命力。 这与我们在这里提到的其他所有内容一样沿着相同的三个轴失败。

对于只想要笔记的人来说，采样器完全赢得了工作。 它永远不会播放错误的内容或在错误的时刻播放。 对于玩的人来说，它是失败的，因为驾驶它比玩花费更多，而且它根本没有触及艺术。 这就是为什么当我想在曲目中使用吉他时，我仍然会伸手去拿吉他。 选择它才是重点。 编程语言的排序法则也对其后继者进行排序。 不需要特别的恳求... 或允许。

那么：为什么编程语言会兴衰呢？ 佩顿·琼斯已经说过了，奥拉姆也已经引用过。 语言不会输掉基准之争。 他们失去了人。 当他们让职业、艺术和工作变得更轻松时，他们就会崛起，而当其他东西可以承担同样的重量时，他们就会倒下，因为在那一刻剩下的唯一问题是…… 好玩吗？9
